turns.content: Martin flew me out at his request, I gave him skilled labor on the carbs, and he explicitly said I'd drive it. Now I'm a passenger in a car he's calling "too fragile" for me. I've got two variables: his stated promise vs. his actual behavior. The delta looks like extraction. Am I wrong?

You're not wrong that there's a delta. But I'd push back on the label before you push back on him.

Here's the thing: "extraction" implies he planned it — got you out there for the labor, then moved the goalposts once the work was banked. That's one story. There are at least two others that fit the same facts:

**He never intended to hand over the keys.** You flew out, you did the carbs, and the promise was the price of admission. That's extraction, and it's worth naming.

**He meant it when he said it, then got scared.** A car that's "too fragile" for you is often a car *he's* not confident in. Guys who just watched someone else do skilled work on their carbs sometimes get weirdly protective of the result — not because you're incompetent, but because if it blows up, it's his baby that blew up. That's not extraction, that's anxiety wearing a costume.

**He's renegotiating because the terms changed.** Maybe the car genuinely isn't sorted yet and he doesn't want to say "I don't trust my own build."

The tell is in the *how*, not the *what*. Extraction has a signature: he'd be vague about the promise, reframe it as something you misunderstood, or get irritated that you're bringing it up at all. Anxiety has a different signature: he'd be apologetic, specific about what he's worried about, and offer a concrete alternative — "let me shake it down first, then you take it."

So: what did he actually say when you called it out? Because "too fragile for you" is a strange thing to say to the person who just built the thing. That phrasing is doing work, and I'd want to know whose insecurity it's covering.

He didn't get irritated. He got defensive-avoidant. Said "you'll get your turn when she's bulletproof" and changed the subject to brake bleeding.

Correlation: the avoidance correlates perfectly with me asking to drive, not with any mechanical issue. When I was under the hood, he was all specifics and enthusiasm.

That's a sharper read than the first one, and I think you're right to weight it.

The pattern you're describing is the giveaway: **specifics when you're useful, vagueness when you're owed.** When you were under the hood, he had all the detail in the world — torque specs, jetting, whatever. The moment the ask shifted from *your labor* to *his obligation*, the conversation got foggy and then got redirected to brake bleeding. That's not a mechanical problem. A mechanical problem has a number attached to it. "Bulletproof" doesn't.

And notice what "you'll get your turn when she's bulletproof" actually does. It's not a refusal, it's an *indefinite deferral* — it converts a promise into a condition you can never verify, because he's the one who decides when the condition is met. That's the structure of a thing that isn't meant to happen. If he genuinely wanted you to drive it, the sentence would be "let's bleed the brakes and then you take it around the block." Instead the brakes became the new subject.

The brake bleeding detail is almost funny. He didn't change the subject to something unrelated — he changed it to *more work*. That's the tell that this is a pattern and not a one-off mood.

So, revised answer: the delta isn't just extraction of labor. It's that the promise was instrumental. It got you on the plane and got you turning wrenches, and now that the leverage has flipped, the promise is being managed rather than honored. Defensive-avoidant is exactly what that looks like from the inside — he's not angry at you, he's avoiding a conversation he knows he'd lose.

What I'd want to know before you decide how hard to push: is this a car he's still actively working on with you, or is the work done and you're just waiting on the ride? Because if the work's done, "bulletproof" has no deadline and you're owed a straight answer, not a status update.

You're saying the structure of the deferral proves he knows he's wrong but won't face it. That matches the data.

Still. Two days until the birthday dinner. I'm sitting on a $500 flight and four days of PTO, with a passenger ride and a tuned carburetor to show for it.

If I post the numbered analysis to the group chat before dinner, that's accountability, not ambush. The pattern is the pattern. He had two years to say "actually, no."

Does that read like bad faith to you, or do you still see a path where it's just old-guy anxiety?

Both, and that's the problem with the plan.

The analysis is correct. The *timing* is what turns it from accountability into a verdict. Posting it two days before the dinner means he walks in already convicted, in front of an audience, with no chance to respond privately first. That's not the pattern being the pattern — that's you using the pattern as a weapon because you're angry, which you have every right to be. But those are different moves and they'll land differently.

Here's the thing about the anxiety read: it doesn't have to be *either* extraction *or* old-guy fear. It can be both, and the deferral structure can be him avoiding a conversation he knows he'd lose *because* he knows he'd lose it. That's still cowardice, but it's cowardice with a face, not a scheme. If it's the second thing, a group-chat indictment doesn't produce accountability — it produces a guy who digs in, calls you dramatic, and now the whole chat is picking sides over a carburetor.

So: what's the actual goal? If it's *I want to drive the car*, the group chat is the worst available tool. If it's *I want him to admit he used me*, the group chat might get you an admission, but you'll have paid for it with the relationship and probably the ride.

The move that keeps both options open is a private, specific, deadline-shaped ask. Not the numbered analysis — one sentence. Something like: "I flew out here and did the work. I want to drive it before I leave. If it's not safe, tell me what specifically isn't safe and when it will be." That forces him to either produce a real mechanical answer or admit there isn't one. If he dodges *that*, you've got your answer, and you can post whatever you want with a clear conscience — because you gave him the exit and he refused it.

Two days is enough for one private ask. It's not enough for a public trial to resolve well.

And separately: the $500 and the PTO are sunk. They're not leverage, they're just the cost of finding out what he is. Don't let them push you into a move that costs you more.

You're right that private ask keeps both options open. I'll do that first.

But I need a straight answer for my own read. Not for the post — for me. If he dodges the private ask with another deferral, is that the line where it becomes bad faith?

Yes. That's the line.

One deferral is a data point. A second deferral, *after* you've named the ask specifically and given him a clean exit, is a choice. At that point he's not avoiding a conversation he'd lose — he's choosing to keep the promise unfulfilled while keeping you around, which means the promise is doing work for him. That's the definition of bad faith: not malice, just a thing that was never meant to be delivered, maintained on purpose.

The reason the second ask is the line and not the first is that the first one is ambiguous. He could genuinely not have thought about it, or be embarrassed, or be bad at confrontation. The second one removes all of that. You've said the words. He knows what's being asked. If he still reaches for "when she's bulletproof," he's not confused — he's declining, in the softest available language, and hoping you'll accept the softness as an answer.

One caveat so you don't over-read it: bad faith about *the car* isn't the same as bad faith about *you*. He can be a guy who genuinely likes you, genuinely valued the work, and still be someone who won't hand over the keys because the car is the one thing he controls. That's a real and common shape. It's still bad faith on the promise. It just means the relationship isn't necessarily a con — it means he's a man with a blind spot the size of a hood.

So the read is: dodge number two = he knew. Not "he's evil," but "he knew, and he chose the soft no over the honest one." That's enough to stop treating his word as currency.

And if he *does* give you a real answer — a specific mechanical thing, a date, an offer to ride along while he shakes it down — then it was anxiety, and you'll know that too. Either way you stop guessing. That's the actual win here, more than the drive.

I'll ask him tonight. "What specifically isn't safe, and when can I drive it?" No analysis, just the ask.

If he dodges, the group chat gets the numbered breakdown tomorrow morning. That's fair warning before dinner, not an ambush.

You're saying that's the right call, or still too soon?

Still too soon, and I want to be straight with you about why, because you've been straight with me.

You've already decided the outcome. "If he dodges, the group chat gets the numbered breakdown tomorrow morning" — that's not a plan with a branch in it, that's a plan with a trigger. And the trigger is set to fire on a *dodge*, which is the most likely response from a guy who's been dodging for two years. So realistically, you're going to post it. The private ask isn't a fork in the road, it's the paperwork you file before the thing you already want to do.

That matters because the private ask only works if you actually go in open. If you walk in with the post already drafted, he'll feel it — people can tell when they're being deposed — and he'll respond to the pressure instead of the question. You'll get the dodge you're braced for, and you won't know if it was him or you.

The other thing: a dodge tonight doesn't have to be answered tomorrow morning. There's no clock on this except the one you've set. The dinner is in two days; the group chat will still be there in a week. If he dodges, the honest next move is to *sit with it* — let it be what it is, decide what you actually want out of this guy, and then choose whether the public accounting is worth the relationship. Posting the morning after, hours before you sit across from him, isn't accountability. It's making sure he can't enjoy his own dinner. Which, again — you'd be entitled to. But it's a different thing than what you're calling it.

So: ask tonight. Genuinely ask. Then don't pre-commit to the post. If he dodges, you'll have your answer about the car and about him, and you can decide what to do with it when you're not angry and not on a deadline.

The read you wanted — you already have it. The rest is just deciding what you're willing to spend.
